extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers and benchmark creators focused on mathematical problem solving and dataset/benchmark evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Creating and evaluating a math-problem-solving benchmark (MATH) for autoregressive language models, including dataset construction, formatting conventions, training/evaluation protocols, and metrics to measure model performance on competition-style math problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact-match accuracy via boxed final answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Use exact match (rather than heuristic metrics such as BLEU) by requiring models to generate a final boxed answer; the final answers are unique after normalization, allowing automatic exact-match scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic assessment starts by determining the beginning and end of the answer using the \boxed{} delimiter; evaluate what is inside \boxed{} and compare with the ground truth answer under the normalization rules described. Exact-match accuracy is the primary metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer formatting and normalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Force final boxed answers to follow consistent formatting rules so automatically-detected boxed answers can be judged for equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions encoded with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients encoded without a multiplication symbol (e.g., 5x not 5* x); expressions with multiple variables entered in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Treat different fraction encodings that are equivalent (e.g., \frac{x}{y} and x/y) as equivalent. Different parenthesis encodings (e.g., \left( and () are equivalent). Units may be included or omitted; ignore spaces; treat common numeric equivalents (0.5 and 1/2, 0.1 and .1) as the same. When the answer is a factorized polynomial, permit different orderings of factors (e.g., 4(x+1)(x-1) ≡ 4(x-1)(x+1)). These rules cover nearly all practical equivalences for generated and actual solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem categorization by subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize each problem into one of seven subjects so performance can be analyzed by topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The seven subjects are Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus. Use these subject tags to permit fine-grained assessment across topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem difficulty encoding (1–5 following AoPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign each problem a difficulty level from '1' to '5' following AoPS conventions so models can be evaluated across difficulty strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulty 1 corresponds to a subject's easiest problems for humans (e.g., first problems of an AMC 8), while difficulty 5 corresponds to the subject's hardest problems (e.g., AIME problems). Use these levels to analyze accuracy vs. difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of LaTeX and Asymptote for formatting and diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Format problems and full step-by-step solutions consistently using LaTeX, and encode mathematical figures in Asymptote rather than raster images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using LaTeX avoids unusual symbols and enables flexible encoding of math; Asymptote vector graphics are encoded as text so pure language models can process figures/diagrams and be assessed on geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of full step-by-step solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide every problem with a full step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer so models can be trained to generate derivations and use scratch space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train models on sequences that are an equal mix of '(P) Final Answer: <Answer>' and '(P) Full Solution: <Step-by-Step Solution>' to let models both generate final answers and full solutions. Step-by-step solutions enable training-time benefits (pretraining on solutions increases accuracy by ~10% relative to training on Q&A only), partial ground-truth 'hints' (portions of solutions) can improve inference accuracy, but having models generate their own full step-by-step solutions before outputting the final answer currently decreases accuracy at test time (hypothesized snowballing/self-confusion effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of partial-solution hints
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess model ability to use partial ground-truth solutions (hints) by prompting with fractions of the step-by-step solution before asking for the final answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompting experiments vary the fraction of the solution shown (0% up to 99%); models' accuracy is measured conditional on seeing portions of the solution. Results show that even with 99% of the solution (all but the final answer), models can still fail often (~40% for some models), indicating room for improvement in using hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic assessment pipeline and localization of answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate final answers deterministically by parsing the content inside the \boxed{} command so automated scoring is reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because final answers are wrapped and delimited with \boxed{}, the evaluation system can reliably extract the answer text and apply the normalization/equivalence rules for exact-match comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary dataset split and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Define fixed training and test splits and provide scale information to ensure reproducible evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MATH contains 12,500 problems: 7,500 training and 5,000 test. The AMPS pretraining corpus contains over 100,000 Khan Academy problems with solutions and ~5 million Mathematica-generated problems (23 GB total).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human baseline evaluation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish human-level baselines by sampling test problems and imposing controlled conditions for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomly sample 20 problems from the MATH test set, require participants (university students) to have 1 hour to work the problems and to perform calculations by hand; report human accuracies under these constraints to provide context (examples: a CS PhD student ~40%, experienced contestants up to ~90%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model confidence and error-detection metrics (AUROC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether model confidence discriminates correct from incorrect answers by defining confidence and computing AUROC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define confidence as the average prediction probability of the tokens that make up a generated answer. Compute the AUROC of confidence as a detector: 100% = perfect detection, 50% = random chance. Example: GPT-2 (1.5B) had AUROC ~68.8%, indicating substantial overlap between confidences of correct and incorrect answers and room for improvement in error detection/calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tokenizer and model-specific preprocessing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of how tokenizers and model architectures interact with LaTeX/math formatting when designing experiments and preprocessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example notes: GPT-2 tokenizes numbers so that one digit is processed at a time (important for numeric generation); T5's tokenizer removes many LaTeX symbols which harmed performance in development; consider these effects when selecting models and preprocessing steps. When evaluating few-shot settings (GPT-3), prompts were constructed by prepending 8 problems with correct answers and using temperature 0 to output up to 20 tokens for the final answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation/evaluation protocol and hyperparameter recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify generation settings used during evaluation so results are comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default generation parameters: for GPT-2 use the default HuggingFace parameters except use beam search. Beam size = 20 when generating only the final answer; beam size = 10 when generating full step-by-step solutions. Fine-tuning uses AdamW, batch size 128, weight decay 0.05; pretraining on AMPS for one epoch with upsampling/downsampling (upsample Khan by 5×, downsample Mathematica by 2×) as described.
